parts.title: Booking a children's holiday club
parts.intro: Part 1. You will hear a father phoning a leisure centre about a holiday activity club for children.

lines: LINDA: Good morning, Westfield Leisure Centre. Linda speaking. How can I help?
MARK: Hi. I'm ringing about the holiday activity club in the summer. My son's seven and my daughter's ten, and I wanted to find out a bit more before I book.

LINDA: Of course. Well, the club runs for the whole of the school holidays, Monday to Friday. It's for children from five up to eleven. We used to take children up to twelve, but we found the older ones wanted different activities, so now there's a separate youth programme for them.
MARK: That's fine, both of mine are in the right range. Where does it actually take place? Is it in the main sports hall?

LINDA: Most of the indoor activities are in the sports hall, yes. But in the morning, please don't bring the children to the main entrance. Parents drop them off at the side entrance, next to the car park, where the staff sign them in.
MARK: The side entrance. OK. And what time does it start?

LINDA: Drop-off is from eight thirty. It used to be nine, but a lot of parents asked for an earlier start so they could get to work on time. The club finishes at four, and there's an after-club option until half past five if you need it.
MARK: That's really helpful. What's the cost?
LINDA: For leisure centre members it's twenty-four pounds a day, per child. For non-members it's twenty-eight.
MARK: We're members, so twenty-four. Are there any discounts?
LINDA: There are. If you book a whole week, Monday to Friday, you get ten per cent off. There's also a reduction for a second child, but I'm afraid that only applies to non-members.
MARK: Right. I think we'll book a whole week, then.
MARK: What do the children need to bring each day?

LINDA: They'll need a packed lunch. We provide drinks and a piece of fruit in the afternoon, but not a full meal. And they should wear trainers, because most of the activities are physical. We don't allow open shoes, even in hot weather.
MARK: OK. And what kind of activities are there?

LINDA: Each day is a bit different. Monday is usually team games, and on Wednesdays they do arts and crafts. Fridays are special, because we take the children on a trip. In previous years we went to the zoo, but it's quite far, and the coach journey was very long, so this summer we're going to a farm instead, only twenty minutes away.
MARK: My son will love that. Is there swimming?

LINDA: Yes, on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The children need to bring a towel and a swimming costume. Goggles are optional. We do a short test on the first day to check which group they should be in, so you don't need to show us a certificate.
MARK: Great. And who should I talk to if I have any questions once it's started?
LINDA: The club leader is Ms Delaney. That's D-E-L-A-N-E-Y. She's at the side entrance every morning, so you can speak to her then.
MARK: Thanks. Can I book online?
LINDA: Yes, you can, through the members' area of our website. You'll just need your membership number.
MARK: Perfect. Thanks very much for your help.
LINDA: You're welcome. Goodbye.

parts.title: A coastal walking festival
parts.intro: Part 2. You will hear a radio presenter talking about a coastal walking festival.

lines: OWEN: Good morning, and welcome to What's On, the weekly guide to events across the county. I'm Owen Price, and this week I'm going to tell you about the Seacombe Coastal Walking Festival, which starts on the twelfth of September.

OWEN: Many people think the festival was started to bring more visitors to the coast in the autumn, after the summer crowds have left. That has certainly been one of the results, but it wasn't the original idea. The first festival, eighteen years ago, was organised by a group of volunteers who wanted to raise money to repair the coastal path, which had been badly damaged by winter storms. A share of every ticket still goes towards looking after the path today.

OWEN: Last year there were thirty guided walks. This year there will be twenty-eight. The organisers had hoped to add some new routes, but a landslip near Gull Point means that two of the usual walks have had to be cancelled, so the programme is a little smaller than usual.

OWEN: Now, booking. In the past, most people booked through the festival website. Unfortunately, the website had a number of problems last year, so this time the organisers are asking people to book by phone, or in person at the tourist office on Harbour Street. You can't just turn up on the day, I'm afraid, because numbers on every walk are limited.

OWEN: A lot of listeners have asked about dogs. Dogs are welcome on many of the walks, but not all of them, because some routes pass through farmland with sheep. If you look at the programme, the walks where dogs are allowed are marked with a paw symbol.

OWEN: And the festival will end, as always, with a special event on the final Sunday. In previous years there was a barbecue on the beach, but because of the dry summer and the risk of fire, it has been replaced this year by an exhibition of photographs taken by walkers during the festival, which will be held in the town hall. Last year's evening concert won't be repeated, as the organisers felt it was too expensive.
OWEN: Let me now pick out five of the walks that I think are particularly worth considering.

OWEN: The Cliff Top Walk is one of the most spectacular, with wonderful views across the bay. However, the path is steep in places and there are long sections without a fence, so the organisers say it isn't suitable for children under twelve.

OWEN: If you'd prefer something gentler, the Harbour Heritage Walk follows the old sea wall around the town. It's completely flat, with a smooth surface all the way, so it's ideal for anyone using a wheelchair or pushing a buggy. It's led by a local historian, and it's full of stories about the town's fishing past.

OWEN: Bird lovers should book the Saltmarsh Bird Walk. You don't need any special equipment for this one: the guides bring telescopes and binoculars for everyone to use. With luck, you'll see thousands of geese arriving for the winter.

OWEN: For something unusual, try the Lighthouse Night Walk. It ends with a visit to the top of the old lighthouse, but because the staircase inside is so narrow, only twelve people can go on each walk, so you'll need to book early. And you'll need to bring your own torch.

OWEN: Finally, the Smugglers' Cove Walk takes you along the shore to a hidden beach that was once used by smugglers. You can't walk back the same way, because the tide comes in and covers the path, so the walk finishes with a short boat ride back to the harbour. Remember to bring a picnic, as there's nowhere to buy food on the way.
OWEN: The full programme is available from the tourist office, and tickets go on sale this Saturday.

parts.title: Planning a noise survey
parts.intro: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Ruth and Amir, discussing a project on noise in their town.

lines: RUTH: So, Amir, we need to decide what to do about the noise project. The first round of measurements didn't really go to plan, did it?

AMIR: Not really. The biggest problem was the timing. We chose the week of the school holidays without thinking, so there was much less traffic than normal. The readings near the schools were really low.
RUTH: Yes, that was a mistake. And the other thing was the weather. It rained on two of the four days, and the meter isn't supposed to be used in the rain, so we lost half our data.
AMIR: At least the equipment itself worked well. I was worried the battery wouldn't last all day, but it was fine.
RUTH: And people were really friendly. I thought residents might not want to talk to us, but almost everyone answered our questions.
AMIR: True. OK, so what should we change in the report? Dr Hughes said our introduction was too long.

RUTH: She mentioned it, but she said it wasn't worth rewriting at this stage. What she really wants is a better method section. We need to explain exactly where we stood and why we chose each place, so that someone else could repeat the study.
AMIR: Right. And she wants us to compare our results with the official noise maps from the council. I didn't even know they existed.
RUTH: Neither did I. I don't think we need more graphs, though. She said we had plenty; they just need clearer labels.
AMIR: What about the conclusion? I thought she might say we'd been too confident.
RUTH: No, she was happy with that, actually. She said it was appropriately careful, given how little data we had.
AMIR: So, for the second round, let's plan it properly. First, I think we should get a map of the area from the council. The one we used was really out of date.
RUTH: Good idea. Their planning office gives them to students for free. Then we choose the sites. Last time, some of our sites were right next to traffic lights, which made the readings jump around.
AMIR: So this time we keep every site at least fifty metres from any junction.
RUTH: Exactly. And before each session, we should calibrate the meter. Last time we did it at home, but Dr Hughes said it should be done in the laboratory, where they have the proper equipment.
AMIR: OK. Then at each site, how long do we record for? We did five minutes last time.
RUTH: The guidelines recommend ten minutes, so that the average is more reliable.
AMIR: Ten it is. And while one of us is recording, the other should count the cars going past.
RUTH: Actually, Dr Hughes said cars don't make much difference. It's the lorries that cause the peaks, so we only need to count those.
AMIR: That's easier. And finally, we put everything into a spreadsheet that we can both edit, rather than writing it in notebooks like last time.
RUTH: Yes, that was a nightmare. And then we can make the graphs straight from it.
AMIR: Great. Shall we start on Monday?
RUTH: Let's check the weather forecast first!

parts.title: Restoring salt marshes
parts.intro: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about salt marshes and how they can be restored.

lines: LECTURER: Today I'm going to talk about salt marshes, which are among the most productive, and the most overlooked, habitats on our coasts.

LECTURER: A salt marsh is an area of flat, low-lying land along a sheltered coast or estuary, which is covered by the sea at high tide. Marshes form where the waves are gentle enough for fine mud to settle, and they're dominated by grasses and other plants that can tolerate salt.

LECTURER: For centuries, people regarded salt marshes as wasteland. In many countries, large areas were drained and turned into farmland, or used for ports and industry. In some estuaries, most of the original marsh has been lost.

LECTURER: Attitudes began to change when scientists started to measure what marshes actually do. One of their most important functions is coastal protection. The dense vegetation slows the waves down, so that by the time the water reaches the sea wall behind the marsh, it has much less energy. This means the walls can be lower, and cheaper to maintain.

LECTURER: Marshes are also important for wildlife. Their creeks act as nurseries for young fish, which shelter there until they're large enough to survive in open water. And in winter, marshes provide feeding grounds for huge numbers of migrating birds.

LECTURER: A third benefit, which has attracted a lot of attention recently, is carbon storage. Marsh plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow, and because the soil is waterlogged, dead plant material decays very slowly. As a result, carbon builds up in the mud over hundreds of years.

LECTURER: So how do you restore a salt marsh? The most common technique is called managed realignment. Instead of maintaining an old sea wall, engineers build a new wall further inland, and then deliberately make a gap in the old one, allowing the sea to flood the land between them.

LECTURER: I'd like to describe one example, at the Elmsworth estuary. Here, the land behind the old wall had been used for growing wheat for about two hundred years. Before the wall was opened, the team had to deal with an unexpected problem: the soil had become so compressed by farm machinery that water couldn't drain through it. They solved this by digging a network of channels, copying the shape of natural creeks.

LECTURER: After the wall was opened, the first marsh plants appeared surprisingly quickly, within a single year. However, the full range of species took much longer to arrive, and birds were slower to return than the team had predicted. Monitoring showed that the main reason was disturbance: a popular footpath ran along the new wall, and walkers with dogs frightened the birds away. The solution was simple. The path was moved a short distance away and screened with a hedge.

LECTURER: Not everyone supported the project. Some local farmers objected to losing productive land, and the scheme only went ahead after an agreement to pay them compensation. Ten years on, though, the marsh has become a popular attraction, and the local economy has benefited from the visitors.

LECTURER: To finish, I want to stress that restoration isn't a quick fix. A restored marsh can take decades to match a natural one, which is why protecting the marshes we still have must remain the first priority.

passages.title: The windcatchers of the desert
paragraphs: Long before electricity made mechanical air conditioning possible, the inhabitants of some of the world's hottest regions devised effective methods of keeping their homes cool. Among the most distinctive is the windcatcher, a tall tower rising above the roofline of a building and designed to capture passing breezes and channel them into the rooms below. Known in Persian as the badgir, the windcatcher is most strongly associated with the desert cities of central Iran, particularly Yazd, where hundreds of towers still punctuate the skyline, although comparable structures can be found around the Persian Gulf, in North Africa and in parts of South Asia.

In its simplest form, a windcatcher consists of a vertical shaft with openings near the top. Air enters through the openings that face the wind, is forced downwards through the shaft and flows into the building, displacing the warmer air already inside. Most towers are divided internally by thin walls, known as partitions, which separate the shaft into several channels, so that air can descend in one channel while it leaves through another. Even in the absence of wind, the tower continues to function to some degree: as the sun heats its upper section, the warm air inside it rises and escapes through the openings, drawing cooler air into the house from below in a process sometimes compared to the action of a chimney.

The most sophisticated windcatchers combined this airflow with water. In certain houses, the incoming air was directed over a pool in the basement or over an underground channel called a qanat, an ancient system of gently sloping tunnels that conveyed water by gravity from distant aquifers at the foot of the mountains. As the water evaporated, it absorbed heat from its surroundings, lowering the temperature of the air before it rose into the living areas of the house. Some households used the resulting cool basement to store perishable food, and in a few localities windcatchers were linked to large domed structures in which ice produced on winter nights could be preserved for use during the summer months.

The design of individual towers varied considerably according to local conditions. Where the prevailing wind blew consistently from a single direction, a tower might have openings on one side only, whereas in districts where winds were variable, towers with four or even eight sides were constructed so as to capture air from any quarter. Height was another important variable, because air moves more rapidly and carries less dust at greater distances above the ground. Taller towers were therefore more effective, but they were also more costly to build, and in some cities regulations restricted their height, apparently to prevent wealthier households from depriving their neighbours of a fair share of the breeze.

Windcatchers were constructed from locally available materials, principally mud brick, which absorbs heat slowly during the day and releases it gradually at night. This property, known as thermal mass, helped to moderate fluctuations in temperature inside the house. The towers did, however, require regular maintenance: openings had to be cleared of sand and debris, and many were fitted with wooden grilles or mesh to prevent birds and insects from entering the shaft and nesting there. Builders also paid close attention to the orientation of each tower relative to neighbouring structures, since an adjacent wall or dome could disrupt the flow of air and substantially reduce its effectiveness.

During the twentieth century, the spread of electric fans and air conditioning led many households to abandon their windcatchers. Some towers were demolished; others survived but fell into disrepair, their openings blocked or their internal walls allowed to collapse. In recent decades, however, architects and engineers have shown renewed interest in the principles behind them, partly in response to the substantial energy consumption and carbon emissions associated with mechanical cooling, which in some hot countries accounts for a large proportion of peak electricity demand during the summer.

Modern interpretations of the windcatcher have been incorporated into schools, offices and public buildings in a number of countries, including several with temperate climates. Contemporary designs frequently use lightweight materials and are equipped with sensors and motorised dampers that regulate the flow of air automatically. Some are combined with heat exchangers, which allow incoming fresh air to be warmed in winter by the stale air leaving the building, so that ventilation is maintained without excessive heat loss.

Engineers caution, nevertheless, that these systems seldom eliminate the need for air conditioning altogether in the hottest climates; rather, they reduce how often and how intensively it is required. Evaporative cooling is also far less effective in humid regions, where the air already contains considerable moisture and the addition of further water vapour can make conditions feel more oppressive rather than less. The windcatcher's lasting lesson may therefore be not that a particular structure should be copied, but that buildings designed in response to their local climate can achieve a great deal with comparatively modest resources.

passages.title: Why waiting feels longer than it is
paragraphs: Most people have experienced the peculiar way in which time appears to stretch while they are waiting: in a queue at a bank, at a bus stop or on hold to a telephone helpline. Researchers who study the psychology of waiting have repeatedly found that individuals estimate the duration of a wait inaccurately, frequently believing that they have waited considerably longer than they actually have. Their satisfaction with a service, moreover, appears to depend more on how long the wait felt than on how long it lasted according to the clock, a finding with considerable implications for the organisations that manage queues. Organisations have consequently begun to treat the experience of waiting as something that can be designed, in much the same way as the products or services that customers are waiting to receive.

One of the most consistent findings in the field is that unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time. A frequently repeated, though possibly embellished, story concerns an office building whose occupants complained persistently about slow lifts. Rather than investing in faster lifts, the managers installed mirrors beside the doors, and the complaints reportedly diminished, apparently because people now had something with which to occupy themselves while they waited. The behavioural scientist Tomas Reyes notes that the same principle underlies the provision of magazines in waiting rooms, entertainment in queues at theme parks and music for callers who have been placed on hold. Researchers have since confirmed the general principle in controlled experiments, in which participants given a simple task to perform consistently underestimated the length of a delay compared with participants who were simply asked to sit and wait. The effect appears to be strongest when the activity is interesting enough to absorb attention but not so demanding that it becomes a burden in itself.

Uncertainty also makes waiting harder to bear. People who do not know how long they will have to wait tend to experience greater anxiety than those who do, and the absence of information can be more distressing than the delay itself. Reyes has found that simply informing people of the expected length of a wait reduces their frustration, even when the wait itself is not shortened. For this reason, many theme parks display estimated waiting times at the entrance to each ride, and these estimates are often deliberately set slightly longer than the actual wait, so that visitors are pleasantly surprised when they reach the front of the queue sooner than anticipated. Telephone helplines have adopted a comparable strategy, periodically informing callers of their approximate position or the expected time remaining, although Reyes cautions that inaccurate estimates can be more damaging than none at all, because they create expectations that are subsequently disappointed.

A sense of fairness is equally important. The economist Priya Anand argues that people judge a wait not only by its duration but also by whether it appears just, and observes that the sight of a later arrival being served first can provoke far more anger than a lengthy but orderly delay. In one of her studies, participants expressed a clear preference for a single queue feeding several service points over separate queues for each, even when the single queue appeared longer, because it guaranteed that customers would be served in the order in which they had arrived. Anand's research also suggests that people are generally willing to accept exceptions to strict order, such as priority for elderly or disabled customers, provided that the reasons are visible and widely regarded as legitimate.

A further factor is the perception of progress. The computer scientist Jonas Feld found that users of a website were considerably more willing to wait for a page to load when a bar advancing across the screen indicated that something was happening, even if the total waiting time was identical. A similar effect has been reported at one airport, where complaints about delays in retrieving luggage diminished after the walk from the arrival gates to the baggage reclaim area was deliberately lengthened. Passengers spent the same total time reaching their bags, but less of that time standing still beside an empty conveyor belt. Feld suggests that the principle applies equally to physical queues: a line that moves forward in small, frequent steps is generally perceived as shorter than one that remains stationary for long periods and then advances in large jumps, even when the overall rate of progress is the same.

Not everyone, however, is comfortable with the way in which these findings are being applied. The ethicist Helena Marsh warns that organisations may use psychological techniques to make customers feel better about delays rather than investing in genuine improvements to their services. In her view, such methods are legitimate only when they accompany real efforts to reduce waiting times, and should never be employed as a substitute for them. She also points out that some techniques, such as displaying a customer's position in an online queue, could be manipulated to discourage people from leaving, a practice she regards as deceptive. Marsh acknowledges, nevertheless, that many techniques are harmless and may genuinely improve people's experience, and she does not oppose their use in principle.

passages.title: Citizen science: the return of the amateur
paragraphs: For most of the history of modern science, the boundary between professional researchers and enthusiastic amateurs was far less distinct than it later became. Many of the most significant contributions to astronomy, botany and geology during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were made by clergymen, physicians and landowners pursuing their interests in their spare time. Over the course of the twentieth century, however, scientific research became increasingly specialised, dependent on expensive equipment and concentrated within universities and government laboratories, and the role of the amateur diminished correspondingly. The recent growth of what is now termed citizen science represents, in some respects, a revival of that older tradition, although it takes a markedly different form.

Citizen science projects typically invite members of the public to contribute to research by collecting or analysing data. Volunteers may record the birds visiting their gardens, report the first flowering of particular plants in spring or classify galaxies in photographs captured by telescopes. The value of such contributions lies principally in their scale. A single research team cannot monitor wildlife across an entire continent, but thousands of volunteers distributed across that area can, and some long-term datasets, including those documenting changes in the timing of spring, have been compiled very largely through records maintained by volunteers. In projects that involve the analysis of images, volunteers can also identify patterns that computer programs still find difficult to recognise reliably. Participation has been made considerably easier by the spread of smartphones, which allow observations to be photographed, located precisely and submitted within seconds, and by online platforms that can coordinate the efforts of volunteers in many different countries simultaneously.

Professional scientists have frequently been sceptical about the quality of data collected by people without formal training, and this concern is not without foundation. Volunteers may misidentify species, record observations inaccurately or report only what they expect to find. Nevertheless, studies comparing amateur and professional data have generally concluded that, for many tasks, the accuracy of volunteers is comparable to that of experts, particularly when tasks are clearly defined and adequate guidance is provided. Many projects now incorporate procedures for verifying data, such as asking several volunteers to classify the same image independently and accepting only those classifications on which most agree.

In my view, a more serious difficulty than accuracy is bias in where and when observations are made. Volunteers tend to record wildlife close to where they live, in accessible locations and in pleasant weather, with the consequence that remote or less attractive areas are underrepresented. Species that are conspicuous or easy to identify are reported more frequently than those that are inconspicuous, and the results can therefore convey a misleading impression of how common particular species are. Statistical techniques can reduce the effects of such biases, although they cannot eliminate them entirely, and researchers need to be explicit about the limitations that remain. Projects that direct volunteers to particular locations at particular times, rather than accepting observations wherever they happen to be made, have been able to reduce this problem considerably, although they tend to attract fewer participants.

Questions have also been raised about the relationship between volunteers and the professionals who analyse their data. In many projects, the public collects information but plays no part in formulating research questions or interpreting results, and volunteers may receive little acknowledgement when findings are published. Some projects have attempted to address this imbalance by naming contributors in academic papers or by inviting them to participate in discussions about how their data should be used. I would go further and argue that, wherever practicable, projects should be designed so that volunteers can propose their own questions as well as gather data to answer other people's. Such arrangements are admittedly more demanding for researchers, who must invest time in explaining their methods and negotiating priorities, but the resulting projects are likely to be more relevant to the communities involved and more sustainable over time.

A small number of projects have already achieved this with notable success, particularly in the monitoring of local environmental problems. Communities concerned about air or water pollution in their neighbourhoods have worked with scientists to design studies, collect samples and present their findings to local authorities, in some cases prompting changes in policy. Such projects demonstrate that volunteers are capable of far more than data collection, and that the expertise they bring, including detailed knowledge of their own surroundings, can complement that of professional researchers. In several cases, residents identified sources of pollution that official monitoring networks, with their small number of fixed measuring stations, had entirely overlooked.

It would be naive to imagine that citizen science can replace professional research, or that every project yields valuable results; some generate data that are never analysed, and others struggle to retain volunteers once initial enthusiasm fades, particularly when the tasks involved are repetitive and participants receive little information about what their efforts have achieved. Yet its potential benefits extend beyond the data it produces. Participants frequently report that taking part has altered the way in which they perceive their surroundings and increased their understanding of how scientific knowledge is generated. At a time when public trust in science is frequently called into question, that experience may ultimately prove to be one of the most valuable outcomes of citizen science.

task1.prompt: The pie charts show how the average household in Norland spent its income in 1995 and 2020. The table shows average household income and size in the same two years. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

figure.title: Norland: household spending and income
figure.alt: Two pie charts and a table. In 1995, Norland households spent 24% of income on housing, 31% on food, 14% on transport, 9% on leisure and 22% on other items. In 2020, the figures were 34% housing, 19% food, 17% transport, 15% leisure and 15% other. The table shows average annual household income rising from 18,500 to 41,200 Norland dollars, and average household size falling from 3.4 to 2.6 people.

task1.model_label: Illustrative model for teacher discussion after the mock. Not a certified band answer.
task1.model:
The pie charts compare the share of income that an average Norland household spent on five categories in 1995 and 2020, while the table gives average household income and size in those years.

Overall, housing replaced food as the largest area of spending, and the proportion spent on leisure grew noticeably. At the same time, households became considerably richer and smaller.

In 1995, food accounted for the biggest share of spending, at 31%, followed by housing at 24%. By 2020, this order had been reversed: housing had risen to 34% of the budget, whereas food had fallen to 19%. The share spent on leisure also increased, from 9% to 15%, and transport rose slightly, from 14% to 17%. In contrast, spending on other items dropped from 22% to 15%.

These changes took place as average annual household income more than doubled, from N$18,500 to N$41,200. Meanwhile, the average number of people in a household fell from 3.4 to 2.6, which may help to explain why a smaller proportion of income was needed for food.

Lexical Resource: Is the language of proportion and change precise (accounted for, the share of, more than doubled, reversed)?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Are past and past perfect forms and comparative structures controlled?

task2.prompt: In many countries, more people now work from home for at least part of the week. Why is this happening? Is it a positive or negative development? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
task2.model_label: Illustrative model for teacher discussion after the mock. Not a certified band answer.
task2.model:
In recent years, working from home has changed from an unusual arrangement into a normal part of many people's working week. In my view, this trend is driven mainly by technology and by employees' changing expectations, and although it creates some difficulties, it is on balance a positive development.

The most important reason for the change is technological. Fast internet connections, video-calling software and shared online documents mean that many office tasks can now be done just as well from a kitchen table as from a company desk. A second reason is that many employers discovered during periods of disruption that their staff could remain productive at home, which removed much of their earlier resistance. Finally, employees themselves increasingly value flexibility. Long, expensive journeys to work are a major source of stress, and many people are no longer willing to accept them five days a week.

There are clear benefits to this development. Workers save time and money on commuting, and parents in particular can organise their day more easily around their children's needs. Companies can reduce the cost of office space, and fewer cars on the roads at peak times means less congestion and pollution. However, there are also disadvantages. Some people feel isolated without colleagues around them, and younger employees may miss the informal learning that happens in a shared office. It can also become harder to separate work from private life.

In conclusion, the growth of home working reflects new technology and new attitudes to work. While employers need to take care that staff do not become isolated, I believe that the freedom and efficiency it offers make it a largely positive change.
checklist: Task Response: Are BOTH questions answered (why it is happening, and positive or negative) with a clear position throughout?
Coherence and Cohesion: Is there a logical paragraph plan, with one main idea per paragraph?
Lexical Resource: Is vocabulary on work and technology precise (commuting, flexibility, productive, isolated)?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Are complex sentences, passives and concessive structures (although, while) controlled?
